issues.legal_issue: A purchaser who acquires land after acquisition proceedings have been notified cannot challenge those proceedings as a subsequent purchaser.
material_facts: The land was notified for acquisition before the appellants purchased it.
The appellants later sought to challenge the acquisition proceedings and the award on the basis of their purchases.
issues.conclusion: The subsequent purchasers could not challenge the acquisition proceedings and were entitled only to seek compensation.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, a transfer after publication of a Section 4 notification does not bind the government, and a subsequent purchaser cannot challenge the acquisition proceedings; upon possession, Section 16 vests the land in the State free from encumbrances. The Court relied on U.P. Jal Nigam v. Kalra Properties (P) Ltd., Sneh Prabha v. State of U.P., Ajay Kishan Shinghal v. Union of India, and Star Wire (India) Ltd. v. State of Haryana.

predicates.subsequent_purchaser_challenges_acquisit: A person who acquired the land after acquisition proceedings began later challenged those proceedings.
predicates.acquisition_notice_preceded_purchase: The acquisition notice concerning the land was issued before the purchaser acquired it.

issues.definition: When a later purchaser challenges acquisition proceedings that were notified before the purchase, the purchaser cannot challenge the acquisition and may seek compensation.

issues.legal_issue: A transfer of land subject to acquisition proceedings is invalid where the required prior written permission was not granted by the authorized competent authority, and registration or mutation does not convey title.
material_facts: The land was subject to acquisition proceedings and had not been released from acquisition.
The appellants or their predecessors transferred the land after acquisition notices had been issued.
The documents relied on as permission or no-objection certificates were not shown to have been issued by the authorized competent authority.
The appellants did not establish that the prescribed applications had been made or that the required inquiry and permission had occurred.
Sale deeds were registered and mutations were granted in the appellants’ favour.
issues.conclusion: The transfers were illegal and without jurisdiction, conveyed no title to the appellants, and the consequential mutations were also without jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4 and 5 of the Delhi Lands (Restrictions on Transfer) Act, 1972 require prior written permission from the competent authority for a covered transfer; Sections 5 and 8 govern the permission process and prohibit registration without that permission. The competent authority was the authority authorized under Section 2(b), not an unauthorized subordinate. Sections 4, 6, 16 and 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 govern the acquisition context and withdrawal from acquisition. The exception permitting transfer must be strictly applied. Under Babu Verghese v. Bar Council of Kerala, following Taylor v. Taylor, Nazir Ahmad v. King Emperor, Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Deep Chand v. State of Rajasthan, and State of Uttar Pradesh v. Singhara Singh, where a law prescribes how an act must be done, it must be done in that manner or not at all.

rule.if: land_subject_to_acquisition and transfer_after_acquisition_notice and prior_written_permission_required and not valid_permission_from_authorized_authority and mutation_granted_on_transfer

predicates.land_subject_to_acquisition: The land was subject to an acquisition proceeding that had not been withdrawn.
predicates.transfer_after_acquisition_notice: The owner or a later holder transferred the land after notice of acquisition had been issued.
predicates.prior_written_permission_required: The governing transfer rules required written permission from the authorized decision-maker before the transfer.
predicates.valid_permission_from_authorized_authori: The authorized decision-maker granted valid written permission before the transfer.
predicates.mutation_granted_on_transfer: An authority entered a mutation in the purchaser’s favour on the basis of the transfer.

issues.definition: When land subject to acquisition is transferred after notice without the required prior written permission from the authorized decision-maker, a resulting mutation does not make the transfer convey title.

issues.legal_issue: An appeal should not be remanded to investigate whether transfer permission existed when the record establishes that statutory requirements were not met, and invalid purchasers are not entitled to alternative land on that basis.
material_facts: The appellants sought a remand for further inquiry into whether a proper application had been made and permission granted.
The record showed no proper application or valid permission from the competent authority, and the appellants failed to prove otherwise.
The appellants also sought directions for allotment of alternative land despite the absence of a valid transfer in their favour.
issues.conclusion: The Court refused to remand the matter and refused to direct allotment of alternative land; it noted that any available statutory remedy could be pursued according to law.
issues.legal_principle: A remand was not warranted where the record established that the required statutory steps had not occurred and the appellants had failed to prove that valid permission was granted. Because no valid transfer conveyed title, there was no basis for directing alternative land to the appellants.

predicates.appeal_seeks_remand_or_alternative_land: A party in an appeal asks for a remand to investigate transfer permission or seeks alternative land based on the purchase.
predicates.record_establishes_permission_requiremen: The record establishes that the required application or permission process did not occur.
predicates.purchaser_fails_to_prove_valid_permissio: The purchaser does not prove that the authorized decision-maker granted valid permission.

issues.definition: When an appeal seeks further inquiry or alternative land but the record shows the required permission process was not followed and the purchaser cannot prove valid permission, remand and alternative-land relief are denied.
